title: Why You'd Never Want To Meet A Leopard Seal

scenes.notes: You're kneeling on Antarctic sea ice, camera up. Orcas leave people alone.
Polar bears? Wrong pole.
Down here, the only thing out to get you is the cold.
Then a penguin shoots out of the water past your boot. Not swimming. Airborne.
Under the ice, a low trill starts, and you feel it through your knees.
A long face rises at the edge of the floe, smiling up at you. That's a leopard seal. It isn't smiling.
It's the only seal in Antarctica that hunts other seals. It plays catch-and-release with live penguins. And in 1916, one came out of the sea after one of Shackleton's men.

props.text: WHY YOU'D NEVER WANT TO MEET ONE

scenes.notes: So let's build the case against ever sharing water with one. And work out why most people who do still climb out fine. Then, the strangest leopard seal story on record. It lasted four days, and nobody got bitten.
Start with size. The biggest leopard seals are the females. A big one can reach about three and a half metres: two of you, lying end to end.
She can weigh around five hundred kilos, about seven of you packed into one torpedo.
Most seals look like sleepy dogs. This one looks like a reptile: long flat skull, head too big for its body.

props.text: NOT A SMILE: A JAW LINE

scenes.notes: And the smile is a trick. The corners of its mouth curve up, so at rest it looks pleased to see you. It's really a jaw that opens very, very wide.
How wide? Wide enough to close over something you'd never expect. We'll get to that.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M60 20 Q80 120 95 180 Q110 120 130 20 Z" fill="#f2efe6" stroke="#9aa" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M190 60 q40 -20 70 10 l0 110 q-30 15 -70 0 Z" fill="#e8c4a8" stroke="#a87" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Its front fangs grow up to two and a half centimetres, about the top joint of your thumb. Puppy face. Crocodile job.

So what fills a mouth like that? Often? Krill. Shrimp-like animals about as long as your little finger. Behind the fangs sit back teeth shaped like little three-pronged forks. Clamp them together and they make a sieve.
In a 2013 study at Sydney's Taronga Zoo, captive seals sucked in water, squirted it out through the gaps and kept the krill.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 600 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 290 L20 110 L300 20 L580 110 L580 290" fill="none" stroke="#e8eef0" stroke-width="8"/></svg>

scenes.notes: That's how a baleen whale feeds, done by an animal that would fit in your garage.
Then it eats everything else: fish, squid, six kinds of penguin, and other seals, up to young elephant seals. The only thing in the sea that hunts a leopard seal is an orca. Picky eater, it is not.

Every penguin colony has a doorway: the strip of water at the ice edge where birds dive in to feed and scramble out to get home. It's also the only way out of the water for you. Station crews even fit guards to their rubber boats, because the seals keep biting the tubes.
Leopard seals know exactly where the doorways are, including yours. One cruises just under the surface along the edge, almost hidden, and waits.
So penguins don't just climb out here. They launch themselves out of the water and onto the ice. That's why the penguin by your boot came out flying.
The ones that don't make it get grabbed, often by the feet, and beaten against the surface. Then the seal whips them side to side to tear off pieces it can swallow.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 500 320" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="10" width="480" height="300" fill="#e9dfc6" stroke="#8a7a5a" stroke-width="4"/><text x="250" y="120" font-family="Georgia" font-size="40" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3a3020">SKINS ITS PREY</text><rect x="60" y="150" width="380" height="8" fill="#b8a888"/><rect x="60" y="178" width="380" height="8" fill="#b8a888"/><rect x="60" y="206" width="380" height="8" fill="#b8a888"/><rect x="60" y="234" width="380" height="8" fill="#b8a888"/><rect x="60" y="262" width="380" height="8" fill="#b8a888"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Older books said it skinned them on purpose. Researchers now think it simply can't chew. Which, if you're the penguin, is not much of an improvement. And that still isn't the strangest thing it does to penguins.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 600 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="900" font-size="30" fill="#fff"><g fill="none" stroke="#6fd6e8" stroke-width="6"><path d="M150 90 A170 120 0 0 1 450 90"/><path d="M450 270 A170 120 0 0 1 150 270"/></g><polygon points="450,70 470,100 430,100" fill="#6fd6e8"/><polygon points="150,290 130,260 170,260" fill="#6fd6e8"/><text x="40" y="190">GRAB</text><text x="430" y="190">RELEASE</text><text x="250" y="40">CHASE</text><text x="255" y="345">GRAB</text></svg>

scenes.notes: Remember that catch-and-release? Divers and film crews have watched leopard seals grab a penguin, let it go, wait for it to race for the ice, and grab it again. Sometimes over and over, without ever eating it. Is it practice? Is it play? Or is it just a seal that's already full, killing time? Honestly, nobody has pinned it down. Which is not a comforting thing to wonder while you're the new thing in its water.

So how does a lone hunter find a penguin, or you, in all that ice and murk? Partly with its face. Like other seals, its whiskers are probably tuned to the faint wakes of swimming animals, and its big eyes suit dim water. And partly, it listens.
Which brings us back to that trill from the start. In the southern summer, male leopard seals sing.

A male hangs upside down, rocking from side to side with his chest pulsing, and calls for hours every day. Those calls reach about 177 decibels underwater, in five distinct types, loud enough to reach you through the ice. Probably to claim space or call in females. Nobody's certain.
Either way, if you can hear one through the ice, there's a big male somewhere below you. And you can't see him.

So go back to your floe. You're kneeling on the exact strip where it waits. Something that eats seals, plays with what it catches, and sings under your feet is looking up at you. You might be worse than prey. You might be interesting.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="90" fill="#cfd6d8" stroke="#7d8a8f" stroke-width="6"/><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="60" fill="none" stroke="#9aa6aa" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Which brings the case file to people. In 1916, Shackleton's crew were stranded on drifting sea ice, eating whatever seals they could catch. Thomas Orde-Lees was skiing back to camp when a leopard seal lunged out of the water at him. He ran. It dived, tracked his shadow from under the ice, and burst up ahead of him. Frank Wild, the second in command, shot it. Then the crew ate it, the most Shackleton ending possible.

In 1985, explorer Gareth Wood was standing on sea ice when a leopard seal burst through, grabbed his leg and tried to drag him in. It bit him twice. His companions kicked it in the head with their spiked boots until it let go.

In July 2003, near Britain's Rothera research station, marine biologist Kirsty Brown was snorkelling with a colleague when a leopard seal pulled her under. It held her under for around six minutes, as deep as seventy metres. Her team could not save her. She was twenty-eight. It is still the only known human death caused by a leopard seal.
Now, a hypothetical, and only that. Your floe tips, and you slide into the water. A long grey shape turns toward you. What can you actually do?
Option one: swim for the boat. Leopard seal bursts are often quoted at around forty kilometres an hour. You, soaked and freezing, might manage three. And remember what it likes to bite on boats.
Option two: climb back onto the ice. That edge is its ambush strip. Gareth Wood was standing on ice when one grabbed him, and Orde-Lees learned it can follow you from underneath.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 120 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M60 12 C30 12 26 50 22 78 L12 92 L108 92 L98 78 C94 50 90 12 60 12 Z" fill="#ffd34d" stroke="#8a6a00" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="60" cy="102" r="10" fill="#8a6a00"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Option three: dive under the floe and hide. Every kick of your legs leaves a wake, and those whiskers are probably tuned to read it. That's hide-and-seek while ringing a bell.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 600 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="900" font-size="30" fill="#fff"><g fill="none" stroke="#6fd6e8" stroke-width="6"><path d="M150 90 A170 120 0 0 1 450 90"/><path d="M450 270 A170 120 0 0 1 150 270"/></g><polygon points="450,70 470,100 430,100" fill="#6fd6e8"/><polygon points="150,290 130,260 170,260" fill="#6fd6e8"/><text x="40" y="190">GRAB</text><text x="430" y="190">RELEASE</text><text x="250" y="40">CHASE</text><text x="255" y="345">GRAB</text></svg>

scenes.notes: Option four: go limp and play dead. This is the animal that catches things, lets them go, and catches them again. Holding still doesn't end the game. It just makes you a quieter toy.

props.text:
THE WATER IS ITS HOME.
THE ICE IS ITS TRAP.

scenes.notes: Which closes the case. If a leopard seal decides you're worth its time, the water is its home, the ice is its trap, and you're out of moves.

And yet, here's what doesn't fit the case. Remember: most people who share its water climb out fine. Scientists have dived near leopard seals for decades, and over a hundred thousand visitors a season now come to Antarctica.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 1600 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="900" font-size="54" fill="#fff" text-anchor="middle"><text x="200" y="80">CIRCLE</text><text x="600" y="80">STARE</text><text x="1000" y="80" fill="#ff5a4a">GAPE</text><text x="1400" y="80">LEAVE</text></svg>

scenes.notes: Almost every meeting in the water ends the same way. The seal circles, stares, opens that huge mouth in what looks like a warning, and leaves.

scenes.notes: One known death, in decades of people working in its water. For an animal this well armed, that's a lot of restraint.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 100 60" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="4" y="4" width="92" height="52" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#e8eef0" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Most of the time, you're not lunch. You're the odd new thing it checks out, like a cat inspecting a box. Which brings us to the strangest leopard seal story of all.

In 2006, photographer Paul Nicklen slipped into the water off the Antarctic Peninsula beside one of those big females, around three and a half metres by his estimate. First she swam straight at him and opened that enormous mouth over his camera. And his head.
Then she backed off, and came back with a penguin. A live one. She let it go right in front of him. When he didn't take it, she tried again. Then she brought them injured, easier to catch. Then dead.

By his own account, she pushed penguins against his lens, blew bubbles in his face when he didn't eat, and kept it up for four days. He came away sure of her verdict. Clumsy thing. Big eye. Can't hunt. Needs feeding. Honestly? Fair review.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 600 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Montserrat" font-weight="900" font-size="30" fill="#fff"><g fill="none" stroke="#6fd6e8" stroke-width="6"><path d="M150 90 A170 120 0 0 1 450 90"/><path d="M450 270 A170 120 0 0 1 150 270"/></g><polygon points="450,70 470,100 430,100" fill="#6fd6e8"/><polygon points="150,290 130,260 170,260" fill="#6fd6e8"/><text x="40" y="190">GRAB</text><text x="430" y="190">RELEASE</text><text x="250" y="40">CHASE</text><text x="255" y="345">GRAB</text></svg>

scenes.notes: Remember the game with the penguins? Researchers who filmed leopard seals sharing a carcass at South Georgia suggest offerings like this might be an offer to cooperate. Either way, the habit that makes this seal frightening is the same one that made it try to look after a person.

So, back on your floe. The rule said only the cold was out to get you. Fair enough: the cold is still far more likely to kill you. But that trill under your knees is a male, singing upside down somewhere below. The penguin that flew past your boot was getting away from something. And the face at the edge of the floe isn't friendly. It's curious. If you're very lucky, lunch is on her.
Walrus or elephant seal: who should we put you in the water with next? Tell us in the comments.
